name: Neutron
info: An atomic nucleus, or a [em1]nuclide[em1], is made of [em2]protons[em2] and [em3]neutrons[em3]. Protons have a positive charge to counteract the negative charge of [em2]electrons[em2] that orbit in shells around the nucleus. Neutrons have [em3]zero[em3] [em3]charge[em3]; that is to say they are neutral.[br] [br]More neutrons in a nucleus do not change an element's chemical properties but they do make it [em1]heavier[em1] and they can affect how [em2]stable[em2] the nuclide is. Nuclides that are not stable [em2]decay[em2] into other nuclides. The measure for how long a given nuclide will last is called its [em3]half-life[em3]. Nuclides decay [em1]at random[em1] so it's impossible to know exactly when a particular nuclide will decay. Instead, how long it takes about half of a bunch of the same nuclide to decay is measurable, and that's what half-life means.[br] [br]The nuclide that is a lone free neutron, [link]Neutron-1[link], has a half-life of about 10 minutes. This means if you had 1000 free neutrons then after ten minutes you could expect to have only 500, and only 250 left after 20 minutes. Neutrons are stable when combined with one or more protons to form an [em1]atomic nucleus[em1].

name: Hydrogen
info: As the very first element [em3]Hydrogen[em3] has only one proton. It's not just first on the Periodic Table, though, it's literally [em1]the first element to exist[em1]. To this day [em2]75% of all the matter in the universe is Hydrogen[em2].[br] [br]Hydrogen on its own is usually a [em1]gas[em1]. The two H's in [em3]H[sub]2[sub]0[em3] are the two Hydrogen atoms, combined with one Oxygen atom, to make [em2]water[em2]. In many common reactions between [em1]acids (like vinegar - C[sub]2[sub]H[sub]4[sub]O[sub]2[sub])[em1] and [em2]bases[em2] [em2](like baking soda - NaHCO[sub]3[sub])[em2], the acid gives a Hydrogen to the base.[br] [br]Hydrogen has two stable isotopes: [link]Hydrogen-1[link] with zero neutrons, also called [em3]Protium[em3], and [link]Hydrogen-2[link] with one neutron, also called [em3]Deuterium[em3] (remember: the number comes from the sum of neutrons and protons). With two neutrons, [link]Hydrogen-3[link] also has a special name: [em3]Tritium[em3]. Tritium has a [em1]half life[em1] of 12.32 years, making it the most stable [em1]radioisotope[em1] of Hydrogen (isotopes that are [em2]radioactive[em2] and decay). All the other isotopes of Hydrogen are very unstable and have half-lives that are only fractions of a second.

name: Helium
info: [em3]Helium[em3] is the lightest [em2]noble gas[em2], meaning it is both incredibly light and very non-reactive. In fact, to make [em1]compounds[em1] with Helium and other elements, it usually requires extreme temperatures or pressures.[br] [br]While Helium is the [em2]second most abundant[em2] element in the universe after [link]Hydrogen[link] it is somewhat rare on Earth because it is so light and non-reactive that it tends to float up to the top of the atmosphere and [em2]escape to space[em2]. Helium also has the lowest [em1]boiling point[em1] of any element, meaning its liquid state is incredibly cold [em2](around 4.2 K, or ​−452° F / −269° C)[em2]. This makes liquid Helium ideal for applications that require extremely low temperatures, such as the [em3]superconducting magnets[em3] used in MRI machines, particle accelerators, and quantum computers.[br] [br]When an atomic nucleus decays by [em3]Alpha (α) decay[em3] it emits an Alpha particle, composed of two [em1]neutrons and two protons[em1]... the same thing as a [link]Helium-4[link] nucleus. This reduces the parent nucleus atomic number by two, for example turning [link]Uranium-238[link] into [link]Thorium-234[link] + [link]Helium-4[link].

name: Boron
info: [em3]Boron[em3] has five protons and isn't made by [em1]fusion inside stars[em1]. Instead it comes from [em1]cosmic ray spallation[em1], where high-energy cosmic rays break apart heavier nuclei, and from supernovas. It's rare in the solar system and makes up only about [em2]0.001% of Earth's crust by weight[em2].[br] [br]Boron has two stable isotopes: [link]Boron-11[link] (about 80% of natural boron) and [link]Boron-10[link] (about 20%). Boron-10 has a high [em2]cross-section for neutron capture[em2], meaning it's very good at [em3]absorbing neutrons[em3]. That makes boron useful in nuclear reactors, in control rods and boric acid, for fission control and emergency shutdown.[br] [br]The same property is used in medicine. In [em1]boron neutron capture therapy[em1], a Boron-10 compound is taken up by a tumor and hit with low-energy neutrons. Each capture releases an alpha particle (a [link]Helium-4[link] nucleus) and a [link]Lithium-7[link] ion, which travel only a short distance, so the damage stays close to the tumor cells.[br] [br]Boron-11 is also a candidate fuel for [em1]aneutronic fusion[em1], a kind of fusion that produces few neutrons. Hit by a proton of about 500 keV, it produces [em3]three alpha particles[em3] and [em3]8.7 MeV of energy[em3].

name: Scandium
info: [em3]Scandium[em3] has 21 protons and one stable isotope, [link]Scandium-45[link], so all natural scandium is the same nuclide. It was made in [em1]supernova explosions[em1] and by cosmic rays breaking apart heavier nuclei. It's about as common in Earth's crust as [link]Cobalt[link], but it's rarely concentrated and mostly comes as a [em2]byproduct of mining[em2].[br] [br]The world makes only about [em2]15 to 20 tons[em2] of scandium a year, but it's put to good use. Adding just a little to [link]Aluminium[link] makes a [em1]stronger alloy[em1] that has been used in Russian MiG fighter jets, baseball bats, bicycle frames, and lacrosse sticks. Scandium is also used in [em3]metal-halide lamps[em3], which make a white light close enough to sunlight for TV cameras to capture good color.[br] [br]Radioactive [link]Scandium-46[link], with a half-life of about 84 days, is used as a [em1]tracer in oil refineries[em1]. [link]Scandium-45[link] is even being studied for a [em2]nuclear clock[em2] that could, in theory, be far more precise than [link]Cesium[link] clocks.[br] [br]Scandium was found in 1879 by Swedish Chemist Lars Fredrik Nilson, and is named after [em3]Scandinavia[em3].

name: Dysprosium
info: [em3]Dysprosium[em3] has 66 protons and [em1]seven stable isotopes[em1], led by [link]Dysprosium-164[link] at about 28% of the natural total. It's also very good at [em2]absorbing neutrons[em2], so mixtures of [em3]Dysprosium Oxide (Dy[sub]2[sub]O[sub]3[sub])[em3] and [link]Nickel[link] are used as control rods in nuclear reactors.[br] [br]But dysprosium is best known for its [em1]magnets[em1]. Replacing a bit of the [link]Neodymium[link] in neodymium magnets with dysprosium (up to 6%) helps them keep their magnetism in demanding uses like [em3]electric vehicle motors[em3] and [em3]wind turbine generators[em3]. An electric car can contain up to 100 grams of it.[br] [br]Dysprosium and [link]Holmium[link] have the highest magnetic strengths of any elements, especially at low temperatures. Dysprosium is also in [em2]Terfenol-D[em2], an alloy that changes shape in a magnetic field more than any other known material at room temperature, and is used in [em1]transducers and fuel injectors[em1].[br] [br]Its name comes from the Greek for [em3]'hard to get'[em3] as its discoverer, French chemist Paul Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran, needed more than 30 attempts to separate it.

name: Iridium
info: [em3]Iridium[em3] has 77 protons and two stable isotopes: [link]Iridium-193[link] (about 63% of natural iridium) and [link]Iridium-191[link] (about 37%). It's formed by rapid neutron capture in [em1]neutron star mergers[em1], and it's one of the least abundant elements in Earth's crust, though much more common in meteorites.[br] [br]That rarity is why a thin iridium-rich layer of clay at the boundary between the Cretaceous and Paleogene periods [em2]66 million years ago[em2] stood out. In 1980 a team led by American physicist Luis Alvarez proposed it came from space, and the idea that a [em3]meteor impact caused the extinction of the dinosaurs[em3] is now widely accepted.[br] [br]Radioactive [link]Iridium-192[link], with a half-life of about 74 days, is used in [em1]brachytherapy[em1] (a form of cancer radiotherapy) and industrial radiography. Iridium is the [em3]second-densest[em3] metal after [link]Osmium[link] and the [em3]most corrosion-resistant[em3] metal known, so it's used in spark plug electrodes and in crucibles for growing crystals. It's named for Iris, the Greek goddess of the rainbow, because its compounds have a [em2]variety of colors[em2].

name: Protactinium
info: [em3]Protactinium[em3] has 91 protons and [em1]no stable isotopes[em1]. The longest-lived, [link]Protactinium-231[link], has a half-life of about 33,000 years, and it's found in nature because it is produced by the decay of naturally-occurring [link]Uranium-235[link].[br] [br]Its name comes from the Greek [em2]protos[em2], meaning 'first', because [link]Protactinium-231[link] decays into [link]Actinium[link].[br] [br]Protactinum also shows up in nuclear energy. In the [em1]thorium fuel cycle[em1], [link]Thorium-232[link] absorbs a neutron and eventually becomes [link]Protactinium-233[link], which decays into [link]Uranium-233[link]. But Protactinium-233 absorbs neutrons too, making it a [em2]neutron poison[em2], so it's removed from thorium reactors as they run.[br] [br]Protactinium is one of the [em1]rarest and most expensive[em1] natural elements, at just a few parts per trillion of the Earth's crust. In 1961, 127 grams of it were extracted from 60 tons of waste. It can also be used for [em3]radiometric dating[em3] of geologic sediments up to 175,000 years old.

name: Nihonium
info: Discoverered at the [em1]RIKEN Nishina Center for Accelerator-Based Science[em1] in Japan, this element was officially named on June 8, 2016. The root of its name, [em3]Nihon[em3], is one of the two ways to say [em3]Japan[em3] in Japanese, literally meaning [em2]the Land of Rising Sun[em2]. Nihonium is the first element to be discovered by an Asian country.

name: Muscovium
info: Officially named on June 8, 2016, [em3]Muscovium[em3] is so named in recognition of the [em3]Moscow[em3] region. This honors the ancient Russian land that is the home of the [em1]Joint Institute for Nuclear Research[em1] where the discovery experiments were conducted using the [em2]Dubna Gas-Filled Recoil Separator[em2] in combination with the heavy ion accelerator capabilities of the [em2]Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions[em2].

name: Tennessine
info: Officially named on June 8, 2016, [em3]Tennessine[em3] is so named in recognition of the contributions of the [em3]Tennessee[em3] region of the United States to superheavy element research. This region is home to the [em1]Oak Ridge National[em1] [em1]Laboratory[em1], [em1]Vanderbilt University[em1], and the [em1]University of Tennessee at Knoxville[em1].

name: Oganesson
info: Officially named on June 8, 2016, [em3]Oganesson[em3] honors [em2]Professor Yuri Oganessian[em2] for his pioneering contributions to research of super heavy elements. Among many acheivements in the field he helped produce experimental evidence for the [em3]island of stability[em3].
